title: What can you say about L-theanine in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 1 wording for L-theanine; the strongest is "Supports a temporary feeling of relaxation" (moderate, 200-250 mg a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Treats or relieves anxiety".

supported_wordings.wording: Supports a temporary feeling of relaxation.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists this use at 200-250 mg a day, citing a few small human studies; no other listed source covers L-theanine.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, total per day. Health Canada sets no timing or duration statement.
supported_wordings.form: L-theanine from tea leaf or synthetic, taken by mouth

wordings_to_avoid.why: Anxiety disorders are diagnosable conditions; the evidence covers a temporary feeling of relaxation, not an effect on a disorder.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: A natural alternative to anti-anxiety medication, or naming a drug such as alprazolam (Xanax)
wordings_to_avoid.why: Compares the product to a drug and implies it does a drug's job.
Promises a cure; the supported effect is short-term relaxation.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
